content: Patients who received linezolid for more than 18 months demonstrated the lowest rates of treatment failure, loss to follow-up, and mortality. Analysis of the relationship between linezolid treatment duration and treatment failure suggests that the optimal duration of use is approximately 20 months, aligning with the typical total duration of a longer multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) regimen. However, this analysis does not account for survivorship bias, as patients who complete the full treatment duration are more likely to have successful outcomes, given that deaths and losses to follow-up tend to occur earlier in the treatment course. No clear pattern was observed between the type of adverse events and the duration of linezolid use. However, a few cases of optic neuropathy, a known complication of long-term linezolid use, were reported. Hematological toxicity, on the other hand, was reported regardless of the duration of use. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) reviewed data from a meta-analysis of adverse events leading to permanent discontinuation of tuberculosis medications or classified as Grade 3–5 severity. Slight differences were noted between the final estimates in the published results and those derived during the GDG deliberations due to the use of an expanded dataset in the publication. These differences, however, did not impact the conclusions regarding the use of these medications. There were insufficient data to estimate risks associated with delamanid, imipenem-cilastatin, and meropenem. Agents not included in Groups A, B, or C were italicized in the guidelines. The 2018 GDG recommended that MDR-TB regimens, where possible, include all three Group A agents and at least one Group B agent, ensuring treatment starts with at least four effective medicines. If bedaquiline is stopped after six months, at least three agents should be continued for the remaining treatment duration. New evidence on the safety of bedaquiline use beyond six months was reviewed by the GDG in 2019. This evidence supports the safety of extended bedaquiline use in patients who undergo appropriate baseline and follow-up monitoring. If only one or two Group A agents can be used, both Group B agents should be included. If a regimen cannot be composed using agents from Groups A and B alone, Group C agents should be added to complete the regimen. In cases where pre-existing comorbidities necessitate early discontinuation of both bedaquiline and linezolid due to health risks, starting with five effective agents rather than four may be advisable. These provisions are expected to apply to most MDR/RR-TB patients, including those with additional resistance to fluoroquinolones or other medicines. The evidence reviewers planned to use advanced analytical approaches to minimize bias, such as marginal structural models and propensity score matching. However, limitations in sample size and dataset constraints precluded full application of these methods. The GDG concluded that residual confounding was likely in the data, and the patient population studied did not allow for extrapolation to routine use in all MDR/RR-TB patients. As a result, no formal recommendation on the efficacy or effectiveness of bedaquiline use beyond six months could be made, though a statement on safety was provided. During the first 203 days of bedaquiline exposure, most drug-related adverse events and serious adverse events occurred. Patients who received bedaquiline for more than 203 days did not experience drug-related adverse events during the initial 203 days of treatment. QTcF values increased by an average of 22 ms during the first month of bedaquiline use but were lower in subsequent months. QTcF prolongation of more than 60 ms from baseline occurred in about 12% of patients, with the highest number of occurrences among those receiving bedaquiline and clofazimine. No events occurred among patients receiving bedaquiline without clofazimine, moxifloxacin, or delamanid. Pregnancy outcomes in bedaquiline-exposed groups included 92% live births, with 8% experiencing fetal or neonatal deaths. The average birth weight of infants exposed to bedaquiline was lower than that of unexposed infants, but this effect could not be conclusively attributed to bedaquiline. Further investigation is needed to explore this relationship. No fatal drug-related events occurred among patients receiving concurrent bedaquiline and delamanid. QTcF prolongation effects of concurrent use were not greater than their additive effects. The GDG noted that QT adverse events in the DELIBERATE trial were surrogate markers of sudden cardiac death. Levofloxacin was the fluoroquinolone of choice in the trial, and serum potassium was closely monitored. The GDG recommended the use of bedaquiline and delamanid in children of all ages. However, challenges exist in reproducing delamanid exposure in young children due to the lack of bioequivalence between the 25 mg pediatric tablet and the 50 mg adult tablet. Splitting the adult tablet may result in shattering, and its contents are extremely bitter and unpalatable. For MDR/RR-TB patients, longer regimens are used when shorter regimens are not feasible. These regimens are more effective when guided by reliable drug susceptibility testing (DST). All MDR/RR-TB patients should be tested for fluoroquinolone resistance before starting treatment. Rapid testing for second-line injectable agents should be performed if amikacin use is considered. DST for other medicines, such as bedaquiline, delamanid, and linezolid, may also inform regimen composition. In settings where DST is unreliable, treatment decisions may rely on clinical history and regional surveillance data. The analysis of treatment duration showed no overall differences in treatment failure or relapse between MDR-TB patients with or without additional second-line drug resistance. However, treatment duration may need to exceed 20 months in cases with extended resistance patterns, depending on clinical response.
